t: You were one cell. Nobody built you. You built yourself, out of that cell, with no plan to look at.
You began as a single cell and assembled yourself into thirty trillion, arranged correctly, with no blueprint anywhere and nothing supervising the process.
sub: Where would the instructions for 'put an eye here' even be kept?
There is no drawing of you anywhere. So what is there instead?

question: If one cell divides into two identical cells, and those divide again, how do you ever get different parts?
Division alone produces copies. Where does difference come from?
options: The cells must end up in different places, and place decides
Each cell is given a different set of instructions
Some cells simply choose to be different
stages.outcome: The cells must end up in different places, and place decides
note: Commit. You already know every cell keeps the identical genome, which rules one of these straight out.

stages.label: Days after the start
captions: Day 0: one cell. Everything you are is in it.
Day 1: two cells. Still identical, still able to become anything.
Day 4: a hollow ball of about a hundred. Still no parts.
Day 15: three layers. Now there is an inside, an outside and a middle.
Day 22: a tube folds up along the back. That becomes your spine and brain.
t: Watch one cell turn into something with a front and a back.
Follow the first three weeks. Note the moment difference first appears, and what it is made of.
after: Nothing differentiated until there were distinguishable positions to occupy. Layers come first, and organs come from layers.

t: Cells become different because of where they end up, not because they were told to.
Cells differentiate according to position. A cell's fate is decided by its neighbours and its location, not by an instruction it was handed.
Differentiation is positional. Identical genomes, different signalling environments, different subsets of genes switched on — which is the previous world's lesson doing structural work.

The logic is local throughout: no cell has any representation of the organism it is part of. Global order emerges from short-range signalling, which is the same class of explanation as the beetle population and the thirty trillion cells that never meet.
sub: The same instructions, read differently depending on where you are.
Every cell keeps the whole genome. Position determines which parts of it get read.
Which is why an early embryonic cell can still become anything, and a late one cannot — the position has not yet been assigned.
Potency narrows as position resolves. Totipotent, then pluripotent, then multipotent, then committed — and each step is the loss of options rather than the loss of information.

q: How does a cell know what to become?
What determines a cell's fate during development?
What is the source of positional information?
options: From where it is and what is next to it
It reads a plan of the whole body
why: There is no plan of you anywhere. A cell can only tell what is right next to it, and that turns out to be enough.
Fate follows position, and position is read from local signals — chemicals reaching the cell and contact with neighbours. No cell has access to any description of the whole.

Positional information is encoded in gradients and contacts, both strictly local. The remarkable part is that purely local rules produce a reproducible global arrangement, which is why development is the best worked example of emergence in biology.

t: Identical twins come from one ball of cells splitting in two, early enough that both halves can still make a whole person.

Monozygotic twinning is exactly this: a split early enough that each fragment still contains cells whose position has not yet committed them. A little later and it is impossible. The window exists because potency narrows as position resolves — which is also why the two are never quite identical, since position is assigned separately in each.
